questions.q: How does this lesson define scalability?
options: A solution's ability to keep working correctly and acceptably fast as data volume and concurrent users grow, not just at launch with a small test data set
A solution's visual polish and page layout design
The number of custom fields an object is allowed to have
How quickly a developer can write the initial version of a feature
questions.explain: Scalability is specifically about sustained correctness and acceptable performance as both data volume and concurrent usage grow over time, not a one-time launch-day measurement.

questions.q: What is the difference between data-volume scalability and concurrency scalability, per this lesson?
options: They are the same concept with two different names

Data-volume scalability concerns how a design behaves as record counts grow; concurrency scalability concerns how it behaves as simultaneous users and transactions grow -- a solution can pass one and fail the other
Concurrency scalability only applies to Experience Cloud sites
Data-volume scalability is entirely Salesforce's responsibility and never a design concern
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates the two axes and gives examples of a solution handling millions of rows fine in aggregate while still choking under heavy simultaneous use, or vice versa.

questions.q: Why does bulkifying Apex that touches more than one record matter for scalability?
options: Apex that queries or performs DML inside a loop can work in a small demo but break or burn through governor limits the first time it processes a real-sized batch
Bulkification is only a stylistic preference with no functional effect
Bulkified code runs exclusively in sandboxes, never in production
Bulkification eliminates the need for any governor limits at all
questions.explain: Non-bulkified logic (queries or DML inside a loop) is a classic pattern that passes small-scale testing and then fails under real data volume, exactly the kind of scalability risk this lesson highlights.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about the naive rollup pattern of recalculating a parent total by querying and summing every child record on every single child update?
options: It scales perfectly at any volume with no changes needed
It's invisible at low volume but becomes a real performance and governor-limit problem as the child object grows large
It is required by Salesforce for all parent-child relationships
It only matters for concurrency scalability, never data-volume scalability
questions.explain: The lesson specifically calls out this pattern as a scalability trap that works fine when the child object is small and degrades as volume grows -- exactly the kind of assumption that needs revisiting as real usage data comes in.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why do scalability failures usually trace back to requirements analysis rather than just 'bad code'?
options: Because code quality has no relationship to scalability at all

Because a scalability requirement -- like expected record volume in three years -- is often never captured during intake, so the design is never built or evaluated against the volume the business actually expects to reach
Because Salesforce automatically handles all scalability regardless of design
Because requirements analysis happens after the code is already written
questions.explain: The lesson ties scalability failures back to Lesson 2's intake questions -- without asking about expected future volume and transaction size, a design can't be evaluated against the scale it will actually need to handle.
